text:
This micro-fiction succeeds by leveraging the uncanny to transform a mundane routine into psychological horror. Creativity lies in the subversion of expectation: suitcases usually imply departure, but here they accumulate, suggesting an inescapable presence or a haunting that grows with each cycle. Coherence is maintained through strict repetition; the train’s rhythm mirrors Mira’s mental state, creating a logical progression from curiosity to dread without needing explicit exposition. Engagement stems from the immediate mystery—who leaves them? Why are they not taken? The brevity forces the reader to fill the gaps, making the silence on the platform louder than any dialogue could be. The final image must shift from observation to implication, turning the passive observer into an active participant in the anomaly.

###FINAL###
Every time the train passed the abandoned station, Mira counted one more suitcase on the platform.

Monday, there was one: a battered leather trunk, brown and dusty. Tuesday, two. A sleek silver carry-on joined it. Wednesday, three. A child’s pink duffel bag sat atop the pile. By Friday, seven suitcases formed a jagged pyramid against the decaying brickwork. No trains stopped here for years. No people walked the tracks. Yet, the luggage multiplied, precise and patient.

Mira pressed her forehead against the cold glass, watching the numbers climb. She tried to ignore them, focusing instead on the blur of trees outside. But the suitcases seemed to pulse in sync with the train’s rhythmic clatter. Ten. Twelve. Fifteen.

On Sunday, as the engine roared past the rusted sign, Mira froze. There were twenty suitcases now. And standing beside the highest stack, facing the speeding train, was a figure wearing her coat, holding her ticket.
